objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer:
Thank you for asking this so honestly — it's exactly the right question to press, and your instinct that "firstborn" *sounds* like it means "born first" is not silly at all. That's genuinely how the English word reads. But here's the key: "firstborn" (Greek *prototokos*) in Scripture is regularly a title of rank and inheritance, not a marker of birth-order. Psalm 89:27 calls David God's "firstborn," though David was neither God's literal son nor firstborn among Jesse's sons — the word there means "preeminent, heir, highest in rank." That's the same usage Paul draws on.

You don't have to take my word for how Paul meant it, though — he tells you himself in the very next verse. Colossians 1:15 calls Christ "firstborn of every creature," and 1:16 immediately explains why: "for by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him." If Christ were himself one of the created things, this sentence collapses into nonsense — the "firstborn" would be creating himself, or Paul would be saying "all things without exception" while secretly meaning "all things except him." Paul isn't being sloppy; he's answering your exact question in advance. The Son is placed on the Creator side of the Creator-creature line, not folded into "all things" as one more creature.

John 1:3 makes the same point with total comprehensiveness: "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made." Not one thing that exists came into being apart from him — so he cannot be among the things that came into being. This is why Christians and Jehovah's Witnesses read Colossians so differently: it comes down to whether "firstborn" is read as a birth-metaphor imported from English, or as the rank-title Paul's own Jewish-Greek vocabulary and immediate argument require. I don't think you're being shown a trick here — you're being shown Paul's own explanation, sitting right there in verse 16.

I've read Colossians 1:15, where Paul calls Jesus "the firstborn of all creation," and I keep coming back to the same worry: doesn't *firstborn* mean he was born—meaning created? I know you're going to tell me it doesn't, but when I read it cold, that's what the word seems to say. And then I think, "If Jesus was created, even if he was created first and greatest, how is he God in the way the Father is?" I guess what I'm really asking is: can you walk me through why Christians read that verse so differently than, say, my Jehovah's Witness coworker does—and do it in a way that doesn't feel like you're hiding something?
